claim: An expanded CAG repeat in the huntingtin gene (HTT) causes Huntington's disease (HD).
source: An expanded CAG repeat in the huntingtin gene (HTT) causes Huntington's disease (HD).
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the field, supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: The length of uninterrupted CAG repeat, not polyglutamine, determines the age-at-onset in HD.
source: Since the length of uninterrupted CAG repeat, not polyglutamine, determines the age-at-onset in HD, base editing strategies to convert CAG to CAA are anticipated to delay onset by shortening the uninterrupted CAG repeat.
evidence: This claim is supported by human genetic data presented in the manuscript showing that age-at-onset correlates with uninterrupted CAG repeat length rather than polyglutamine length.

claim: Base editing strategies employing combinations of cytosine base editors and guide RNAs (gRNAs) efficiently converted CAG to CAA at various sites in the CAG repeat without generating significant indels.
source: Base editing strategies employing combinations of cytosine base editors and guide RNAs (gRNAs) efficiently converted CAG to CAA at various sites in the CAG repeat without generating significant indels, off-target edits, or transcriptome alterations, demonstrating their feasibility and specificity.
evidence: This is supported by MiSeq data showing CAG-to-CAA conversion and analysis showing no significant increase in indels compared to controls.

claim: Candidate BE strategies converted CAG to CAA on both expanded and non-expanded CAG repeats without altering HTT mRNA and protein levels.
source: Candidate BE strategies converted CAG to CAA on both expanded and non-expanded CAG repeats without altering HTT mRNA and protein levels.
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot analysis and RNAseq data showing no changes in HTT expression levels.

claim: Somatic CAG repeat expansion was significantly decreased in the liver by a candidate BE strategy treatment in HD knock-in mice carrying canonical CAG repeats.
source: In addition, somatic CAG repeat expansion, which is the major disease driver in HD, was significantly decreased in the liver by a candidate BE strategy treatment in HD knock-in mice carrying canonical CAG repeats.
evidence: This is supported by fragment analysis data from treated mice showing reduced expansion index.

claim: CAG repeat expansion was abolished entirely in HD knock-in mice carrying CAA-interrupted repeats.
source: Notably, CAG repeat expansion was abolished entirely in HD knock-in mice carrying CAA-interrupted repeats, supporting the therapeutic potential of CAG-to-CAA conversion strategies in HD and potentially other repeat expansion disorders.
evidence: This is supported by fragment analysis comparing interrupted and uninterrupted repeat mice.

claim: Most HD subjects carry an uninterrupted glutamine-encoding CAG repeat followed by a glutamine-encoding CAA-CAG codon doublet (referred to as a canonical repeat).
source: Most HD subjects carry an uninterrupted glutamine-encoding CAG repeat followed by a glutamine-encoding CAA-CAG codon doublet (referred to as a canonical repeat) (Ciosi et al., 2019; Genetic Modifiers of Huntington's Disease (GeM-HD) Consortium, 2019; Wright et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous genetic studies.

claim: The age-at-onset of HD subjects carrying loss of interruption or duplicated interruption is best explained by the length of their uninterrupted CAG repeat, not the encoded polyglutamine length.
source: Surprisingly, the age-at-onset of HD subjects carrying loss of interruption or duplicated interruption is best explained by the length of their uninterrupted CAG repeat, not the encoded polyglutamine length (Ciosi et al., 2019; Genetic Modifiers of Huntington's Disease (GeM-HD) Consortium, 2019; Wright et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations and data analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: The HTT CAG repeat shows increased repeat length mosaicism in the target brain region.
source: This mechanism provides a good explanation of the relationship between CAG repeat length and age-at-onset in HD very well as (1) the HTT CAG repeat shows increased repeat length mosaicism in the target brain region (Telenius et al., 1994; Shelbourne et al., 2007; Mouro Pinto et al., 2020)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Somatic instability is repeat length-dependent.
source: (2) somatic instability is repeat length-dependent (Mouro Pinto et al., 2020; Ciosi et al., 2019)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The levels of repeat instability shows correlations with cell type-specific vulnerability and age-at-onset.
source: (3) the levels of repeat instability shows correlations with cell type-specific vulnerability and age-at-onset (Shelbourne et al., 2007; Mouro Pinto et al., 2020; Swami et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The majority of onset modification signals represent instability-related DNA repair genes.
source: In addition, somatic repeat instability of an expanded HTT CAG repeat appears to play a major role in modifying HD since our genome-wide association (GWA) studies have revealed that the majority of onset modification signals represent instability-related DNA repair genes (Genetic Modifiers of Huntington's DiseaseConsortium, 2015; Genetic Modifiers of Huntington's Disease (GeM-HD) Consortium, 2019; Hong et al., 2021; Lee et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to GWA studies.

claim: Loss of interruption accounts for 0.23% of disease chromosomes in HD subjects.
source: Loss of interruption alleles lack the CAA interruption. This repeat is infrequent in Huntington's disease (HD) subjects (0.23% in our GWAS data)
evidence: This is based on data from the authors' previous GWAS studies.

claim: Duplicated interruption accounts for 0.76% of disease chromosomes in HD subjects.
source: Duplicated interruption alleles, featuring two copies of the CAA-CAG, are also infrequent (0.76% in our GWA participants)
evidence: This is based on data from the authors' previous GWAS studies.

claim: The age-at-onset of loss of interruption carriers is best explained when three CAGs were added to the true CAG repeat length.
source: The age-at-onset of the loss of interruption carriers (n=21) was best explained when three CAGs were added to the true CAG repeat length (Figure 1—figure supplement 3)
evidence: This is based on least square approximation analysis performed by the authors.

claim: The duplicated interruption carriers behaved with respect to age-at-onset as if they had one less CAG than their true CAG repeat length.
source: while the duplicated interruption carriers (n=69) behaved with respect to age-at-onset as if they had one less CAG than their true CAG repeat length (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on least square approximation analysis performed by the authors.

claim: Converting a canonical repeat with 43 uninterrupted CAGs to a duplicated interruption by converting the 42nd CAG to CAA would delay age-at-onset by approximately 12 years.
source: For example, if a duplicated interruption is generated from a canonical repeat with 43 uninterrupted CAGs by converting the 42nd CAG to CAA using BE strategies, the age-at-onset is predicted to be delayed by approximately 12 years (Figure 1D)
evidence: This is based on calculations using the observed effects of duplicated interruption on age-at-onset.

claim: BE4 exhibited high levels of C-to-T editing activity on the target sites harboring NGG PAMs.
source: BE4 exhibited high levels of C-to-T editing activity on the target sites harboring NGG PAMs (Komor et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The activity window of BE4 is positions 4–8, counting from the PAM distal end of the spacer.
source: The activity window of BE4 is positions 4–8, counting from the PAM distal end of the spacer (where the PAM is positions 21–23) (Figure 2B; Koblan et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work and illustrated in a figure.

claim: The nucleotide preceding the target cytosine affects the C-to-T conversion efficiency in cytosine base editors, especially when a G precedes the C.
source: The nucleotide preceding the target cytosine also affects the C-to-T conversion efficiency in cytosine base editors, especially when a G precedes the C (Komor et al., 2016; Kim et al., 2017a; Gehrke et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: An evolved CDA1-based BE4max variant (evoCDA1) showed substantially higher editing on GC targets.
source: For instance, an evolved CDA1-based BE4max variant (evoCDA1) showed substantially higher editing on GC targets (Thuronyi et al., 2019)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: HEK293 cells carry two canonical repeats (16 and 17 CAGs).
source: Our MiSeq sequence analyses revealed that HEK293 cells carry two canonical repeats (16 and 17 CAGs) and showed approximately 10% of basal levels of indel (Figure 3—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is based on MiSeq sequencing data from the authors' experiments.

claim: Transfection of plasmids for BE strategies did not significantly increase the levels of indels compared to cells without any treatment or cells treated with empty vector.
source: Nevertheless, transfection of plasmids for BE strategies did not significantly increase the levels of indels compared to cells without any treatment (Cell) or cells treated with empty vector (EV) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on MiSeq data analysis comparing treated and control cells.

claim: BE4max in combination with gRNAs 1, 2, 5, and 7 resulted in efficient CAG-to-CAA conversion.
source: For example, BE4max in combination with gRNAs 1, 2, 5, and 7 resulted in efficient CAG-to-CAA conversion (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is based on MiSeq data showing increased CAG-to-CAA conversion.

claim: BE4-NG robustly produced CAG-to-CAA conversions with gRNAs 1, 2, and 3.
source: The BE4-NG robustly produced CAG-to-CAA conversions with gRNAs 1, 2, and 3; although not significant, gRNAs 5 and 7 also generated high levels of CAG-to-CAA conversions (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on MiSeq data analysis.

claim: BE4-SpG with the combinations with gRNAs 1 and 2 resulted in significant levels of CAG-to-CAA conversions.
source: BE4-SpG with the combinations with gRNAs 1 and 2 resulted in significant levels of CAG-to-CAA conversions (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on MiSeq data analysis.

claim: The CAG-to-CAA conversion was higher in evo-SpG compared to other base editors.
source: Overall, the CAG-to-CAA conversion was higher in evo-SpG compared to other base editors; gRNAs 1, 2, 4, and 8 produced significant CAG-to-CAA conversions (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on MiSeq data comparing different base editors.

claim: BE4max, BE4-NG, and BE4-SpG in gRNA 1 showed the most conversion at the second CAG with decreased levels of conversion at the first CAG.
source: The patterns of conversion sites were similar for BE4max, BE4-NG, and BE4-SpG in gRNA 1, showing the most conversion at the second CAG with decreased levels of conversion at the first CAG (Figure 4A, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is based on analysis of MiSeq data showing conversion sites.

claim: evo-SpG-gRNA 1 combination showed higher editing efficiencies with the maximum conversion at the second CAG with comparable levels of conversions at the 1st and 3rd CAGs.
source: In contrast, evo-SpG-gRNA 1 combination showed higher editing efficiencies with the maximum conversion at the second CAG with comparable levels of conversions at the 1st and 3rd CAGs (Figure 4A, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is based on analysis of MiSeq data showing conversion sites.

claim: BE4-NG and BE4-SpG produced modest but significant levels of duplicated interruption in combinations with gRNAs 5 and 7.
source: However, BE4-NG and BE4-SpG produced modest but significant levels of duplicated interruption in combinations with gRNAs 5 and 7 (0.5–1% increase over the basal levels) (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on MiSeq data analysis.

claim: gRNAs 1 and 2 showed relatively smaller numbers of predicted off-targets due to unique sequences near the PAMs.
source: The gRNAs 1 and 2 showed relatively smaller numbers of predicted off-targets due to unique sequences near the PAMs (Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is based on Off-Spotter analysis.

claim: One and four genes were predicted off-target sites for gRNA 1 and gRNA 2, respectively, and all showed low levels of conversion compared to on-target.
source: For gRNAs 1 and 2, we experimentally evaluated predicted off-targets focusing on protein-encoding genes; one and four genes were predicted off-target sites for gRNA 1 and gRNA 2, respectively, and all showed low levels of conversion compared to on-target (Supplementary file 6).
evidence: This is based on experimental validation of predicted off-targets.

claim: gRNAs 1 and 2 showed low-level conversions in the CAG repeats of other polyglutamine disease genes in general.
source: As predicted, gRNAs 1 and 2 showed low-level conversions in the CAG repeats of other polyglutamine disease genes in general (Figure 4—figure supplement 6, Supplementary file 8).
evidence: This is based on MiSeq analysis of CAG repeats in other genes.

claim: gRNA 1 and gRNA 2 produced modest CAG-to-CAA conversion on both mutant and normal HTT in patient-derived iPSC and differentiated neurons.
source: Then, gRNA 1 and gRNA 2 produced modest CAG-to-CAA conversion on both mutant and normal HTT (approximately <3%; Supplementary file 9).
evidence: This is based on sequencing analysis of treated iPSC and neurons.

claim: A candidate BE strategy (BE4max-gRNA 1) did not increase the levels of in-frame insertion/deletion in the mutant or normal HTT repeat.
source: A candidate BE strategy (i.e. BE4max-gRNA 1) did not increase the levels of in-frame insertion/deletion in the mutant or normal HTT repeat (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: This is based on analysis of HEK293-51 CAG cells.

claim: BE4max-gRNA 1 produced high levels of CAG-to-CAA conversions on both expanded and non-expanded repeats.
source: Subsequent analysis revealed that a candidate BE strategy BE4max-gRNA 1 produced high levels of CAG-to-CAA conversions on both expanded and non-expanded repeats (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is based on MiSeq analysis of HEK293-51 CAG cells.

claim: Conversion was significantly higher in the non-expanded repeat compared to the expanded repeat.
source: Although very modest, conversion was significantly higher in the non-expanded repeat (uncorrected p-value, 0.04996), which can be explained by slightly reduced conversion on the mutant HTT due to higher GC content in the expanded CAG repeat.
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of MiSeq data from HEK293-51 CAG cells.

claim: The candidate BE strategies did not alter huntingtin protein levels at the time of treatment.
source: However, the candidate BE strategies did not alter huntingtin protein levels (Figure 5E and F) at the time of treatment, supporting the safety of candidate BE strategies.
evidence: This is based on immunoblot analysis.

claim: Candidate strategies such as BE4max-gRNA 1 and BE4max-gRNA 2 produced significant on-target CAG-to-CAA conversions.
source: Candidate strategies such as BE4max-gRNA 1 and BE4max-gRNA 2 produced significant on-target CAG-to-CAA conversions (Figure 6A)
evidence: This is based on MiSeq analysis of HEK293 cells used for RNAseq.

claim: The levels of HTT mRNA were not altered by either BE4max-gRNA 1 or BE4max-gRNA 2 treatment.
source: but the levels of HTT mRNA were not altered by either treatment (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on RNAseq data analysis.

claim: Neither BE strategy induced significant gene expression changes in any genes (false discovery rate, 0.05).
source: In addition, RNAseq data analysis showed that neither BE strategy induced significant gene expression changes in any genes (false discovery rate, 0.05) (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on differential gene expression analysis of RNAseq data.

claim: Somatic CAG repeat expansion index in the liver of HD knock-in mice carrying around 110 CAGs showed a positive correlation with the inherited CAG repeat length and the age of mice.
source: As expected, somatic CAG repeat expansion index in the liver of HD knock-in mice carrying around 110 CAGs showed a positive correlation with the inherited CAG repeat length (as represented in tail DNA) and the age of mice (Figure 7A and B; Pearson et al., 2005; Mouro Pinto et al., 2020; Wheeler et al., 1999; Kacher et al., 2021; Kennedy and Shelbourne, 2000; Lee et al., 2011).
evidence: This is based on fragment analysis of liver samples from HD knock-in mice.

claim: Retro-orbital injection of AAV9 for split cytosine base editor and gRNA 2 significantly decreased the levels of repeat expansion when the effects of the tail CAG repeat size and age of mice were corrected.
source: However, when the effects of the tail CAG repeat size and age of mice were corrected, retro-orbital injection of AAV9 for split cytosine base editor and gRNA 2 significantly decreased the levels of repeat expansion (Figure 7C; p-value, 1.78E-6).
evidence: This is based on linear regression analysis of expansion index data from treated and control mice.

claim: HD knock-in mice carrying 105 interrupted CAG repeat showed complete loss of repeat expansion compared to 105 CAG uninterrupted repeat mice.
source: HD knock-in mice carrying 105 interrupted CAG repeat (https://www.jax.org/strain/027418) showed complete loss of repeat expansion compared to 105 CAG uninterrupted repeat mice (https://www.jax.org/strain/027417; Figure 7D and E)
evidence: This is based on fragment analysis comparing interrupted and uninterrupted repeat mice.

claim: CAA interruption could completely suppress the most important disease modifier (i.e. CAG repeat expansion).
source: suggesting that CAA interruption could completely suppress the most important disease modifier (i.e. CAG repeat expansion).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that interrupted repeat mice showed no expansion.

claim: BE employing nickase Cas9 does not intentionally create double-stranded DNA breaks (DSBs).
source: BE employing nickase Cas9 does not intentionally create double-stranded DNA breaks (DSBs) (Komor et al., 2016; Gaudelli et al., 2017), minimizing potential adverse effects.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work on base editing.

claim: The majority of well-characterized disease-causing mutations are point mutations.
source: The majority of well-characterized disease-causing mutations are point mutations, and therefore many genetic disorders can be addressed by BE strategies (Rees and Liu, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: The robustness of BE has been demonstrated in models of genetic disorders caused by point mutations.
source: The robustness of BE has been demonstrated in models of genetic disorders caused by point mutations (Villiger et al., 2018; Koblan et al., 2021; Rees and Liu, 2018; Newby et al., 2021)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The first human trial employing BE has already been started.
source: and the first human trial employing BE has already been started (Kingwell, 2022; Eisenstein, 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to news articles.

claim: Genetically supported targets significantly increase the success rate in clinical development.
source: First, genetically supported targets significantly increase the success rate in clinical development (Nelson et al., 2015; King et al., 2019; Hingorani et al., 2019)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: BE strategies were derived directly from human genetic observations in HD individuals.
source: our BE strategies were derived directly from human genetic observations in HD individuals, (Ciosi et al., 2019; Genetic Modifiers of Huntington's Disease (GeM-HD) Consortium, 2019; Wright et al., 2019) pointing to the uninterrupted CAG repeat length in HTT as the most direct therapeutic target in HD.
evidence: This is based on the rationale for the study derived from human genetic data.

claim: If BE strategies are applied to fully penetrant 40 or 41 CAG canonical repeats, the repeats can become reduced penetrant (i.e. 36–39).
source: In addition, if BE strategies are applied to fully penetrant 40 or 41 CAG canonical repeats, the repeats can become reduced penetrant (i.e. 36–39).
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the mechanism of CAG-to-CAA conversion.

claim: BE strategies may be able to convert some of the reduced penetrant CAG repeats (e.g. 36 and 37 CAG) to non-pathogenic (CAG<36), which can prevent the manifestation of the disease.
source: Similarly, BE strategies may be able to convert some of the reduced penetrant CAG repeats (e.g. 36 and 37 CAG) to non-pathogenic (CAG<36), which can prevent the manifestation of the disease.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the mechanism of CAG-to-CAA conversion.

claim: CAG-to-CAA conversions in the experiments occurred on both mutant and normal HTT.
source: Although CAG-to-CAA conversions in our experiments occurred on both mutant and normal HTT, our candidate BE strategies are expected to produce mutant allele-specific consequences.
evidence: This is based on experimental data showing conversion on both alleles.

claim: The amino acid sequence and levels of huntingtin were not altered by BE strategies.
source: The amino acid sequence and levels of huntingtin were not altered, while the length of the uninterrupted CAG repeat was decreased.
evidence: This is based on immunoblot and RNAseq data.

claim: On the mutant allele, shortening of the uninterrupted CAG repeat is expected to reduce the somatic instability, lowering its disease-producing potential.
source: On the mutant allele, this shortening is expected to reduce the somatic instability, lowering its disease-producing potential.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the relationship between CAG repeat length and instability.

claim: On the normal allele, inherited variation in the length of the CAG repeat has not been associated with an abnormal phenotype.
source: On the normal allele, inherited variation in the length of the CAG repeat has not been associated with an abnormal phenotype (Lee et al., 2012), so the shortening of the CAG repeat is expected to be benign.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: BE strategies can achieve allele-specific consequences without relying on individual genetic variations beyond the CAG repeat.
source: Importantly, the mutant allele-specific consequences can be achieved without relying on individual genetic variations beyond the CAG repeat.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the mechanism of action.

claim: BE strategies can be applied to all HD subjects without targeting SNPs.
source: Our BE strategies can achieve allele-specific consequences without targeting SNPs, and, therefore, can be applied to all HD subjects, representing a huge advantage over SNP-targeting allele-specific strategies.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the mechanism of action.

claim: BE with relaxed PAM requirements has increased the applicability of BE.
source: Lastly, BE with relaxed PAM requirements Walton et al., 2020; Rees and Liu, 2018 has increased the applicability of BE, and our study has further expanded the target space of this powerful technology.
evidence: This is supported by citations and the demonstration in this study.

claim: BE is appropriately viewed as a tool to correct disease-causing point mutations or to modify gene expression by introducing early stop codons or altering splice sites.
source: BE is appropriately viewed as a tool to correct disease-causing point mutations or to modify gene expression by introducing early stop codons or altering splice sites (Rees and Liu, 2018; Kuscu et al., 2017; Kim et al., 2017b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: This study demonstrates that base conversion can address disease-causing repeat expansion mutations without involving DSB.
source: However, our study demonstrates that base conversion can address disease-causing repeat expansion mutations without involving DSB.
evidence: This is based on the experimental results showing CAG-to-CAA conversion without significant indels.

claim: The BE strategies evaluated did not robustly generate duplicated interruption that are found in humans.
source: The BE strategies that we evaluated did not robustly generate duplicated interruption that are found in humans, potentially due to the possibility that PAM at specific sites that are required to generate duplicated interruption did not sufficiently support the activity of cytosine base editors that we tested.
evidence: This is based on MiSeq data showing modest levels of duplicated interruption.

claim: The inability to directly target putative toxic species such as RAN translation or exon 1A huntingtin fragment may represent one of the limitations of BE strategies for HD.
source: Also, the inability to directly target putative toxic species such as RAN translation or exon 1A huntingtin fragment (Yang et al., 2020; Neueder et al., 2017; Bañez-Coronel et al., 2015; Sathasivam et al., 2013) may represent one of the limitations of our BE strategies for HD.
evidence: This is a logical inference about potential limitations.

claim: If the levels of alternative toxic species are dependent on the length of uninterrupted CAG repeat, CAG-to-CAA conversion strategies may be able to ameliorate toxic species-mediated HD pathogenesis.
source: Still, if the levels of those alternative toxic species are dependent on the length of uninterrupted CAG repeat, CAG-to-CAA conversion strategies may be able to ameliorate toxic species-mediated HD pathogenesis.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential benefits.

claim: BE strategies may not produce any significant clinical benefits if they are applied too late in the disease.
source: Although BE strategies can address the primary disease driver in principle, they may not produce any significant clinical benefits if they are applied too late in the disease.
evidence: This is a logical inference about timing of treatment.

claim: There is evidence for significant levels of neurodegeneration at the onset of characteristic clinical manifestations.
source: Considering the evidence for significant levels of neurodegeneration at the onset of characteristic clinical manifestations (Paulsen et al., 2008), CAG-to-CAA conversion treatments may not produce any clinical improvements if applied late.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: BE strategies can be applied quite early without involving deficiency-related adverse effects because CAG-to-CAA conversion is predicted to neither alter the amino acid sequence nor changes the expression levels of HTT.
source: With the expectation of mutant-specific consequences, we reason that BE strategies can be applied quite early without involving deficiency-related adverse effects (Lopes et al., 2016; Rodan et al., 2016; Dietrich et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2016) because CAG-to-CAA conversion is predicted to neither alter the amino acid sequence nor changes the expression levels of HTT.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the mechanism of action and supported by citations about deficiency effects.

claim: The expansion-decreasing effects of initial AAV injection experiments may have been limited compared to cell culture systems by inefficient delivery and difficulty in targeting the repeat sequence.
source: The expansion-decreasing effects of our initial AAV injection experiments, while significant, may have been limited compared to cell culture systems by inefficient delivery and difficulty in targeting the repeat sequence.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparing in vitro and in vivo results.

claim: Efficient delivery methods will be critical for the successful application of BE strategies to human HD.
source: For the successful application of BE strategies to human HD, efficient delivery methods will be critical.
evidence: This is a logical inference about requirements for clinical translation.

claim: The ideal levels of CAG-to-CAA conversion that produce significant clinical benefits are currently unknown.
source: Currently, the ideal levels of CAG-to-CAA conversion that produce significant clinical benefits are unknown.
evidence: This is an explicit statement about the current state of knowledge.

claim: A series of preclinical studies using relevant model systems may generate data that may shed light on the optimal conversion rate levels that are required to produce significant clinical benefits.
source: A series of preclinical studies using relevant model systems may generate data that may shed light on the optimal conversion rate levels that are required to produce significant clinical benefits.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about future research needs.

claim: Developing base editors with high levels on-target gene specificity and minimal off-target effects is a critical aspect to address.
source: In addition, developing base editors with high levels on-target gene specificity and minimal off-target effects is a critical aspect to address (Li et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Adverse effects due to immunogenicity are issues that may hamper the application of BE strategies to humans.
source: Also, adverse effects due to immunogenicity are issues that may hamper the application of BE strategies to humans.
evidence: This is a statement about potential challenges.

claim: Thorough assessments of immune responses against BE strategies and subsequent modification will be critical to address immune response-associated safety issues of BE strategies.
source: Thorough assessments of immune responses against BE strategies (e.g. development of antibody, B cell, and T cell-specific immune responses) and subsequent modification (e.g. immunosilencing) (Ewaisha and Anderson, 2023) will be critical to address immune response-associated safety issues of BE strategies.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work on immunosilencing.

claim: Age-at-onset of duplicated interruption carriers is significantly delayed compared to that of loss of interruption carriers with the same uninterrupted CAG repeat size even though duplicated interruption encode four more glutamines than loss of interruption.
source: Furthermore, age-at-onset of duplicated interruption carriers is significantly delayed compared to that of loss of interruption carriers with the same uninterrupted CAG repeat size even though duplicated interruption encode four more glutamines than loss of interruption (Student's t-test p-value, 1.007E-12) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of age-at-onset data from HD subjects.

claim: Striatal and liver repeat instability share certain underlying mechanisms.
source: Since striatal and liver repeat instability share certain underlying mechanisms (Mangiarini et al., 1997; Manley et al., 1999; Kovtun and McMurray, 2001; Kennedy et al., 2003; Kovalenko et al., 2012; Pinto et al., 2013; Ament et al., 2017; Loupe et al., 2020), and in vivo delivery might be more efficient in the liver compared to the brain (Levy et al., 2020), we used AAV9 to evaluate a candidate BE strategy in the liver.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In vivo delivery might be more efficient in the liver compared to the brain.
source: and in vivo delivery might be more efficient in the liver compared to the brain (Levy et al., 2020)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The modified sequence in the treated mice could not be determined by sequencing because of very long CAG repeats, modest levels of base conversion, and high levels of errors when sequencing the CAG repeat.
source: Unfortunately, we could not determine the modified sequence in the treated mice by sequencing because of (1) very long CAG repeats in these mice, (2) modest levels of base conversion, and (3) high levels of errors when sequencing the CAG repeat.
evidence: This is an explicit statement about technical limitations.

claim: Insufficient dosage due to difficulty in producing high titer viral package for big cargo, limited delivery, and/or difficulty in targeting the very long CAG repeat resulted in modest effects of BE treatment in mice.
source: We speculate that (1) insufficient dosage due to difficulty in producing high titer viral package for big cargo (i.e. 5 KB) (Levy et al., 2020; Wu et al., 2010), (2) limited delivery (Carvalho et al., 2017), and/or (3) difficulty in targeting the very long CAG repeat resulted in modest effects.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about reasons for modest effects, supported by citations.
